```text
Peak Poker Performance

not miss out on the most important details, no matter how subtle. The
best players don’t. Even if you consider yourself a recreational player,
take note of how much time you spend being fully aware when you play.
If you are watching sporting events, checking your phone, or playing
Open Face Chinese Poker on your iPad, by definition you cannot be fully
absorbed in the game.
    More than any other factor, attention is at the center of the peak per-
formance puzzle. Being able to focus is a key skill because what we pay
attention to influences our thoughts, feelings, and behaviors and even im-
pacts the neural pathways in the brain. B. Alan Wallace, author of The At-
tention Revolution, said, “Few things affect our lives more than the fac-
ulty of attention. If we can’t focus our attention – we can’t do anything
well.” Of course, it is a given that it is impossible to stay 100% focused all
of the time. The mind is a natural wanderer. Because of this human limita-
tion, we need to become especially good at detecting when we have lost
focus so that we can refocus ourselves back on the task at hand.
    It is also a biological fact that your mind can only be productive in the
past or the present or the future. It cannot be in more than one place at a
time. While at the table, keep your mind on the present and firmly on the
process of playing well. If you notice that your mind has wandered, simply
bring it back to the present.

Developing Situational Awareness
Up until now I have stressed self-awareness, but there is another aspect
of attention that will serve you well: situational awareness. This is an un-
derrated aspect of the A game. Self-awareness is a great first step to-
wards optimal performance, but if you want to be totally in the zone, you
have to attend to what is going on around you. Situational awareness
simply means that you are able to assess, absorb, and respond to infor-
mation effectively.
   The three phases to situational awareness are being able to:

     ♠ Perceive what is happening around you; observing betting patterns
        and being aware of opponents’ emotional states are examples.
```

```text
                                             Deconstructing the A Game

   ♠ Make sense out of the information that you note; comprehending
       information is not always a simple task, but it is necessary if you
       want to achieve peak performance.
   ♠ Take effective action on what you have gleaned.

   There are some players who like to describe themselves as “feel” play-
ers. In most cases they are actually high in situational awareness. By being
incredibly alert and attentive to environmental cues they are able to put
the pieces of the puzzle together in a way that appears seamless.

The Myth of Multi-tasking
We would all like to believe that we are great multi-taskers, but when it
comes to being fully focused, multi-tasking is a myth. The brain naturally
focuses on concepts one at a time in a sequential fashion. Research is
very clear on this point. We are biologically incapable of processing “at-
tention-rich inputs simultaneously” (Medina, 2008).
   According to Medina, there is a four-step process that occurs in the
brain when we try to multi-task:

   ♠ A shift alert: this is when something comes into our awareness,
       blood rushes to our anterior prefrontal cortex, and alerts the brain
       that it’s time to shift attention.
   ♠ Rule activation: when the brain finds the neurons that are capable
       of addressing what was brought to its attention in the shift alert.
   ♠ Neuron activation: once the brain finds the proper neurons, it must
       rouse them into action. This process takes several tenths of a
       second to accomplish.
   ♠ Disengagement: when a new distraction comes in, your brain must
       disengage from what you are doing before it can look for the
       neurons needed to address this new information. Once it’s
       disengaged, it finds and rouses the proper neurons, and you refocus
       on the new distraction. This takes another few tenths of a second.
```

```text
Peak Poker Performance

   These four steps occur every single time you switch from one task to
another. It doesn’t sound as if this takes much time, but the time adds up
and can be significant. Since a large part of the A game is centered around
focus and attention, do yourself a favor and stop trying to multi-task. Re-
search shows that when people repeatedly switch tasks they make more
errors than if they concentrate on a few tasks. Create an interruption-
free zone while you are playing, and reap the benefits.

Two Paths to Increasing Your A Game Rating
In general, there are two strategies for increasing time in your A game
rating. The first is essentially a strategy of addition: focus on doing more
of what works. Figure out what you are doing when you are playing your
best, and seek to do more of it. When you use an addition strategy, you
are attempting to add things to your game. Constant tweaking and im-
proving can help you, tremendously.
    Average players play mindlessly, instead of focusing on each hand indi-
vidually and making decisions based on the specifics of the hand or situa-
tion. The best players are always analyzing and making adjustments. If you
are a recreational player you have to develop your technical skills in order
to increase your time playing your A game – but there is a sizable mental
component, too. You want to put yourself in the position of making the
best possible decisions every time you sit down at the table. You must be
fluent in your tools (Flopzilla, Equilab, etc.) and your equities. In fact, in Se-
crets of Professional Tournament Poker, Vol. 1, Jonathan Little stressed
that you need to know the hand equities like the back of your hand. The
more time you put into the development and refinement of your poker
skills, the more likely you are to be able to perform at the top of your game.
    The second strategy is one where you reduce the time you spend in
the C, D, or F part of your game. Often it is easier to eliminate errors than
to master peak performance. Eliminating mistakes is an underappreciated
way to improve. Cutting the downside is often a faster approach to win-
ning more, because it doesn’t require that you master a new level of play.
Let me show you why.
```

```text
                                            Deconstructing the A Game

    Imagine that you have tracked your results meticulously, and discov-
ered that when you are playing your A game you can achieve a win rate of
5bb/100. What does your F game lose rate look like? Maybe your records
indicate that when playing your F game you lose 10bb/100. You can see
that even a small amount of time playing your F game completely wipes
out your A game profit. You could also lose a lot more in your F game than
that! Twenty or 30bb/100 losses are not unusual. If you are using a sub-
traction strategy of improvement, you’ll do everything in your power to
lop off your D and F game. The easiest way to do this is to sit out when-
ever you notice that your game has devolved.
    How do you know if your game has devolved to the point where you
should either take a break or leave altogether? It goes back to being self-
aware. If your awareness has slipped and you are missing important de-
tails, it may be time to go. Getting sloppy in your decision making can be
another sign. Going on autopilot could be a hint as well. Whenever we go
on automatic pilot, we increase the chance that we will react to triggers
in unconscious and habitual ways. We want to make certain that we take
every opportunity to consider all options before choosing the best one.
The ability to pause before reacting is the key to self-discipline.
    Another aspect to consider is that most people do not like to get up
when they are losing. They want to chase their losses. You have to re-
member that you are practicing a subtraction strategy that helps you
keep more money in your pocket over the long haul. This piece of advice
is so important that it bears repeating. If you play 90% of your hands well
but 10% poorly and those 10% are large errors, you could end the session
an overall loser!
    In summary, if you are making errors and getting frustrated, consider
getting up or at the very least instituting a stop-loss. Some players make
a rule that they will leave as soon as they are down one or two buy-ins.
On the other hand, if you are in a soft game where your C level is better
than their A game, by all means stick around.
```

```text
Peak Poker Performance

Strong Emotions and the A Game
Having strong emotions at the poker table impacts the A game in many
ways. They can cause erratic play, which can lead to losses and missed
opportunities for profit. It’s possible to become mentally and emotionally
hijacked when strong emotions are evoked at the table. Now let’s turn our
attention to some of the most common strong emotions that affect the
way you play.
    If you feel too positive, you may play too loose. You’ll let down your
guard, become lackadaisical when you need to maintain diligence and ob-
jectivity. Maybe you’ll ignore things you shouldn’t. You might get over-
confident, which can lead you to ignore sound bankroll management.
Some players start to play a sloppy, undisciplined game when they’re run-
ning hot. Also, be on guard for boredom. It is not possible to play your A
game when you are bored or distracted.
    If you feel angry, you may be motivated by revenge. Anger arises from
an event that we experience as unfair or unjust. If anger surges un-
checked, we are likely to act rashly and do something we regret. Acting
rashly to get revenge in order to “show them” is emotionally unintelligent
poker. Be aware that this form of emotional hijacking is very common.
    In any case, once your actions and reactions become emotionally
driven, high levels of arousal and an inability to focus is the result. It starts
when you make game decisions based on emotions rather than in accor-
dance with careful assessment. Feelings-driven actions that seem correct
at the time are seen in hindsight as obviously wrong. Attention narrows
and excludes virtually all other considerations and possibilities from our
thought process. It’s almost as if we are possessed!
    There is a direct link between poker behavior and emotional state. You
need to understand how your emotions affect your game. How you play is
likely to be significantly impacted by your emotional reactions to both
your successes and setbacks. Big wins can lead to euphoria and unwar-
ranted confidence. Big losses can lead you to play more cautiously and
even sub-optimally.
```

```text
                                              Deconstructing the A Game

major challenge for many poker players. You have to get used to the idea
that being emotionally uncomfortable while playing is okay. You’ll some-
times experience frustration, doubts, worries, and anxiety while you are
playing. You’ll also occasionally feel stress – but you can still make good
profitable decisions. Getting comfortable with discomfort is something
that elite players are able to do masterfully.
   Because poker involves incomplete information and situations that are
unique, there is always a level of uncertainty and thus a level of psycho-
logical discomfort in making plays. The discomfort diminishes considerably
as you gain experience, but it is still there. Fear, anxiety, and frustration
are part of being human and very much a part of poker.
   Fear is such a common complaint that I want to spend a bit more time
on it. There are many different sources of fear that come up in poker –
fear of success, fear of failure, fear of being judged, fear of loss, and fear
of being wrong, to name just a few. Let’s look at a couple of common
fears and see how they typically play out at the table.
   No one likes to be wrong; it bruises our ego. We make excuses for our
mistakes. Instead of honestly assessing the situation so that we can
change, we get stuck rationalizing. We all like to perceive ourselves fa-
vorably and being wrong hurts our view of ourselves. It’s also easy to
imagine what our friends and family will think when they see us losing.
This is especially true when your identity and reputation are tangled up
with how you perform as a player and with your wins and losses. It’s a
strong human need to look good (even if it’s only to ourselves), and it is
hard, but not impossible, to override this need.
   Some players have a strong fear of losing. No one likes to lose money,
but it’s an inescapable part of poker. There is no method of playing that
doesn’t lose some money, at least some of the time. Poker is probabilistic,
and any given hand has a probability that it will win or lose. If we play
hands that are +EV (expected value) in +EV spots, we will be long-term
winners. Still, there will always be losing hands, and losing can hurt. It can
promote irrational actions and thoughts. We do things to avoid losses,
```

```text
Peak Poker Performance

attempt to override the probabilistic laws of poker. When we act out of
this fear, we are trying to prevail over a fundamental principle of poker,
which simply cannot be done. It is a losing battle that many poker players
find difficult to disengage from.
      Feeling fearful or anxious at the table can engender thoughts like, “I’m
really afraid of a big loss” or “I’m afraid of long periods of run bad.” Such
thoughts encourage self-doubt, frustration, and feeling badly about your-
self. Keep in mind that fear is not just a feeling; it affects our actions. If
you can identify fear as it begins to emerge, you can choose effective
steps to deal with it before you become overwhelmed.
      You’ll become a winner when you learn to separate your ego needs
from winning money. You must be able to accept losses and mistakes as a
natural part of game flow. You can’t will things to happen.
      Also, notice that thinking thoughts like “I’ve had too many losses lately,
I’ll just book a small win” or “I have to make up for last week’s loss” can
cause more anxiety. Instead of thinking objectively about the game you’re
in or the quality of your opponents, you focus on your internal state!
      Anxiety is a major stumbling block that can prevent peak poker per-
formance. Generally speaking, anxiety at the poker table boils down to
one of three factors:

   ♠ lack of confidence in your ability to perform up to your own
       desires
   ♠ lack of confidence in your ability to perform up to the
       expectations of significant others, like friends or family
   ♠ fear of losing money.

    If you are fully immersed in playing, you won’t find yourself thinking
about the above mentioned potential troubles. Also, if you lack confidence
in your abilities, the best remedy is to put in the work to strengthen your
game. The development of confidence comes from learning the nuances of
poker and having success at applying your newfound skills and knowledge.
```

```text
                                             Deconstructing the A Game

    It may be difficult to get over the fear of losing money, as it seems to
be hardwired into most of us. However, recognize that poker becomes
infinitely psychologically easier when you adopt the attitude that losses
are a natural and unavoidable part of the game. Experience has shown
that less experienced players tend to be more emotionally reactive and
less adaptive in their responses when losses occur. If you can learn to ac-
cept losses with grace, you’ll go a long way in reducing your anxiety in this
area.

Assessing Emotional Responses
How should you respond to your emotions at the table, then? It is critical
that you shine a light on your issues, because gaining self-awareness is
the first step to improvement.
    What emotions do you typically experience as you are playing? Do you
notice irritation, anger, or frustration? Maybe you begin to feel defeated
and depressed when you’re running bad. Conversely, do you get overly
happy or excited when you’re running good?
    What happens when you have a strong emotion? We have a much bet-
ter chance of doing something constructive with strong feelings, when
they are just beginning to crop up. We have less chance to act positively,
if we have already been hijacked.
    How do you experience tilt?
    Take a close look at how you feel, and what thoughts are running
through your mind when you start to tilt. It’s vital that you become aware
of what you are saying to yourself as you grow more emotional. Are you
viewing the game and your situation objectively, or is fear, anxiety, frus-
tration, and/or anger driving you? Here are useful questions to think
about for your assessment:

   ♠ What was the exact event or situation that triggered the
       emotion(s)?
   ♠ What specific thoughts were you thinking that ignited or amplified
       your strong emotional response?
```
